vignette:
Bao, a 27-year-old journalist, presents as articulate and composed, yet a deep exhaustion is evident in the set of his shoulders. The events that brought him to therapy occurred eight months ago, but for Bao, they have never truly ended. The trauma was an assault by his then-partner, a man whose volatility had been escalating for months. The final night began with a tense, quiet bus ride home from a friend's dinner. Bao remembers the feeling of the worn vinyl seat under his hands, the dread coiling in his stomach with every stop, knowing an argument was inevitable. The explosion happened just after they got off the bus, on the dimly lit street leading to their apartment. An accusation, a shove, and then a flurry of blows that left Bao on the cold pavement, a sharp, radiating pain in his ribs and a profound sense of shock.

In the months that followed, the world began to shrink. The bus became an impossible space; the squeal of air brakes or the rumble of an engine outside his newsroom window is enough to make his heart pound. He now takes expensive ride-shares or walks, adding an hour to his commute and significant strain to his finances. As a journalist, his work requires him to meet and interview people, often one-on-one. He now finds any meeting where he is alone with a man to be an exercise in controlled panic. He focuses on the exit, maps the distance to the door, and can barely retain the details of the conversation, convinced that you can never truly know who might harm you. This has made his work feel precarious, his once-sharp interview skills blunted by overwhelming fear. His editor has commented on the declining quality of his recent pieces.

The memory of the assault is not a coherent narrative he can recall at will; it is a sensory ambush. A story on the news about a local dispute can trigger it, and suddenly he is no longer in his apartment but back on that street. The memory feels intensely present, as if it is happening right now, complete with the phantom ache blooming in his side, a somatic echo of the real impact. The wave of shame and terror that accompanies it is so overwhelming that he has to physically stop what he is doing, often retreating to the bathroom to grip the sink until the world solidifies around him again.

At night, sleep offers little respite. He frequently wakes in a cold sweat, heart racing, and feels compelled to check the locks on the doors and windows, peering through the blinds into the empty street below. His new partner, Minh, is gentle and reassuring, but Bao finds that even when Minh tells him he is safe, the words feel hollow. He has come to believe that people simply can't be trusted, that a calm surface can hide anything. This conviction plays out in agonizing ways; if Minh is ten minutes late coming home from work, Bao’s mind doesn’t conjure images of traffic but of betrayal or disaster. He has learned to smother any flicker of his own anger, viewing it as a dangerous, volatile force that must be suppressed at all costs.

This vigilance is fueled by a relentless internal monologue of self-blame. He spends hours ruminating on what he must have done wrong to provoke the attack, convinced that he is fundamentally inadequate. This belief manifests in a quiet, punishing form of control: restricting his food. Some days he eats very little, the feeling of hunger a familiar, grounding distraction from the emotional chaos. He came to therapy after a weekend away with Minh, a trip that was meant to be restorative but was instead marred by Bao’s constant anxiety and inability to relax. He saw the hurt and confusion in Minh’s eyes and realised he was destroying the first safe relationship he had known. What frightens him most is the thought that he is permanently broken, but what he hopes for is to one day feel safe in his own body, in his own home, again.
